title: Reflection at plane and curved surfaces — mirrors
topicTitle: Reflection at plane and curved surfaces — mirrors
notes: The law of reflection says the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in one plane, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal.
A plane mirror forms an image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. The image is virtual, upright and the same size. Left and right appear swapped because the image faces the object.
A concave mirror converges parallel rays to a real focus. Its focal length is half the radius. In the Cartesian convention a real object has negative u, and a concave mirror has negative f.
The mirror formula in that convention is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. A negative v means a real image in front of the mirror. Magnification is −v/u, and a negative value means the image is inverted.
A convex mirror has a positive f in this convention and always gives a virtual, diminished, upright image for a real object. It is used as a driving mirror because the field of view is wide.
An object at the centre of a concave mirror, u = 2f, produces a real inverted image at the centre, the same size. That is a quick check of the formula.

universalFacts: Lens maker: 1/f = (μ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). Power P = 1/f (dioptre, f in metres); lenses add powers in contact.
Refraction at a plane surface (Snell): n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂. Total internal reflection when θ > θ_c, sinθ_c = n₂/n₁ (n₂<n₁).
Prism minimum deviation: n = sin((A + D_min)/2)/sin(A/2). Achromatic doublet pairs crown (low Abbe) + flint (high Abbe).

keyPoints: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
A concave mirror can form a real image.
Cartesian u is negative for a real object.
summary: Reflection equates the angles from the normal. A plane mirror gives a virtual image as far behind as the object is in front. A concave mirror uses 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with negative f, and an object at the centre is imaged at the centre, real and inverted.
